h1: Website calls to action that bring taproom bookings
title: Website Calls to Action for Bookings | Craft Beer School
desc: How to place calls to action that bring taproom bookings: what to say on the button, where to put it, how to keep forms short and how to test.
teaser: A visitor who wants to book should never have to look for the button. Small changes to wording and position add up.
standfirst: A call to action is the one thing you want a visitor to do next. For a taproom that is usually to book a table, join a tour or find the door. Here is how to make it easy.
sections:
Decide the single most useful action for each page and make it obvious. A visit page should lead to a booking or directions. A beer page should lead to where to buy or to the taproom. An events page should lead to a ticket or reservation.

Secondary actions such as joining a newsletter can sit lower on the page. If five buttons compete, none wins.

Write the button text to tell the visitor what they get. Book a table for four works better than Submit. See the tap list tells the visitor what they will find. Avoid wording that sounds like pressure or promises. Never suggest that drinking more earns a reward.

Add a short line below the button that removes doubt: free to cancel, a reply within a day, no payment now. Only say what is true.
Place it where the decision happens

Put the main call to action near the top of the page, so a visitor on a phone sees it without scrolling. Repeat it after the content that persuades, such as after the description of the tour. On a phone, a button that stays in view as the visitor scrolls can help, as long as it does not cover the content.

Make buttons large enough to tap with a thumb, with space around them. Use a colour that stands out against the page.

Every field you add loses some people. For a table booking you need a name, a contact, a date, a time and a number of guests. Ask for the rest later. Show a clear confirmation message after booking. Send a confirmation email or message as well.

Collect only the personal data you need, say what you will use it for and follow the privacy rules that apply where you operate. For events that involve alcohol, state the age policy plainly and check age at the door as the law requires.

Many people still call to book. Show your phone number as text, set as a tap-to-call link. State the hours when someone will answer. Make sure the number matches your Business Profile. Answer messages promptly; a booking request ignored for a day is often lost.
Test one change at a time

Change one thing, such as the wording of the button. Compare the count of bookings over a few weeks against the weeks before. Do not draw big conclusions from a handful of bookings. Weekends, holidays and events all swing the numbers, so compare similar periods.

Record every change with its date, so you can tell what helped. Count with the tools in measuring website leads.
Calls to action beyond the booking

Not every visitor is ready to book. Offer a gentler step too: see the tap list, get directions, join the mailing list for event news. Keep these visually quieter than the main action so they do not compete.

For trade visitors such as bars and shops, give a separate path: a trade enquiry form or a named contact. A bar manager should not need to scroll through a consumer page to find how to order.

Where your site covers more than one venue, make the booking route specific to each, with the right address, hours and phone number on the same page.

Accessibility matters too. Buttons should have clear text, enough contrast against the background and a size that works for everyone. Make forms usable with a keyboard and clear about errors. People with low vision, older visitors and anyone in bright sunlight on a phone all benefit. Accessible design is also good for conversions, because a page that is easy to use is easier to act on.

Print the same clear route on posters and menus: a QR code that opens the booking page, not the home page. Check that the code works on an ordinary phone in dim light.

Once a month, try to book from a phone, on mobile data, as a stranger. Time it. Does the page load quickly? Is the button visible? Does the confirmation arrive? Fix what slows you down. Also see content that brings visitors for the pages that lead to the button.
faqs: Use them rarely. A pop-up that covers the page on a phone frustrates visitors and can hurt how search engines see the page.
Say the action and the result: Book a table, Reserve a tour, See opening hours. Avoid vague words like Submit.
How do I know a change worked?
Count bookings before and after over similar periods. Change only one thing at a time.
